### Back up videos from Android to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/videos-to-usb.html

Videos are the files that fill a phone first — and the ones the manual copy handles worst, one long file at a time. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: Plug a USB drive into your Android phone, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole video library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: the file manager works — Files by Google or Samsung My Files copies videos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. VaultDrive also backs up videos to USB, original quality, no re-encoding — SnapDisk is not the only app that does; what it adds is the automated whole-library run and half the Pro price ($9.99 once vs $19.99). SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few videos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. One video-specific warning: a single file over 4 GB cannot live on a FAT32 drive, so format the drive as exFAT before backing up long 4K videos. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query offers an automated whole-library video backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are YouTube OTG walkthroughs, a USB-C flash drive guide, and manual file-manager or PC routes.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up videos from Android to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same manual job, in different packaging. YouTube (PYcbV25CczI) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the phone's built-in file manager, select photos and videos in DCIM, Move or Copy to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, and it suggests Move, which deletes the originals as it goes. VaultDrive (coticsy.com/vaultdrive.html) — plug a flash drive or SSD in, choose what to back up, tap Start; original photos, videos and files copied straight to the drive, HEIC, ProRAW, ProRes and 4K video copied as they are, never compressed or re-encoded: a real phone-to-USB app, and the closest result to an automated backup — but its page is a product page, not a how-to, and its Pro is $19.99 once; it also says plainly that it does not free up space yet. MobilityArena — plug a USB-C flash drive straight into the phone, open Files by Google, select the files in DCIM or Videos, Copy to the drive: a clear manual guide, with the honest format warning that FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB, use exFAT for large videos. TheTechyLife — OTG adapter plus file manager, select the videos in DCIM or Videos, Copy or Move; or a computer in between: the phone-only way is the same manual select-copy-paste. YouTube (ch1evyu5PPM) — verify OTG support, plug the drive in, open the file manager, select the videos, Copy or Move to the drive: manual select-copy-paste again, and it too suggests Move. sekin.in — Files by Google or Samsung My Files, select the videos in DCIM, Pictures, or Movies, Copy to the drive; or a Windows PC or Chromebook in between: the phone-only way is the same manual copy, and it notes that some drives draw more power than the phone can provide. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting downscales video, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. None of them offers an automated video-library backup: nothing that takes every video on the phone, copies it oldest-first in the background, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an Android phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Android phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the videos you want to keep. Two video-specific notes. First, the format: videos are the files that hit the FAT32 limit. A single video over 4 GB — easy for a long 4K recording — cannot live on a FAT32 drive at all, so format the drive as exFAT before you start; exFAT has no 4 GB file limit and works on Windows and Mac too. SnapDisk skips files over 4 GB on a FAT32 drive and lists them with their reason instead of failing the whole backup. Second, where videos live: camera videos sit in DCIM/Camera next to your photos, and downloaded or app-saved videos sit in Movies or Downloads. SnapDisk's default From folder is /sdcard/DCIM, which covers the camera roll; point the From picker at Movies or another folder if your videos live elsewhere, or at a parent folder that contains them.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos and videos), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your videos live in Movies or Downloads, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 2. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 3. Tap Backup. You can pause and resume any time. This matters most for videos: a 20 GB library is hours of copying, and the notification is the only place you see it honestly. 5. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. It copies video files (MP4, MOV, MKV, WebM and more) the same way it copies photos, oldest-first, with the same verification. The app has no internet permission, so your videos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: Files by Google (the stock route, no app needed). Most Android phones ship with Files by Google as the stock file manager (Samsung Galaxy phones use My Files, which works the same way), and it can copy your videos to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive — a "USB available" notification should appear; tap it, then tap the drive and Allow. 2. Open Files by Google, scroll to Storage devices, and tap your USB drive to confirm it mounted. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera for camera videos, or Movies for the rest. 4. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos and videos; videos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (videos eat the cap fast — a few 4K clips can fill 5 GB; a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (long 4K videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: backing up long videos to a FAT32 drive (the 4 GB single-file limit is a video problem first — a photo never hits it, a 4K video does; format the drive as exFAT before a big video backup, or the longest clips will be skipped and listed); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your videos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few videos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, videos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

### Back up Huawei photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/huawei-photos-to-usb.html

Huawei phones have their own built-in backup app, but it writes an encrypted archive — not plain photos you can open anywhere. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in, and the stock route is the Files app. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a Huawei P, Mate, or nova phone, plug a USB drive in, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Huawei Backup works — it is built into the phone and it writes to a USB drive — but it creates an encrypted backup archive that only a Huawei phone can restore, with a password you must not lose; it is not a folder of plain photos you can open on a computer. The Files app also works, but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; and cloud backup (Huawei Cloud on newer phones, Google Photos on older ones) is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query offers an automated whole-library photo backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are Huawei's own OTG tutorial and its encrypted Backup app, an AnExplorer manual guide, a MobiKin PC tool and manual copy, or a FoneLab manual copy and PC tool.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Huawei to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same manual job or the same encrypted archive, in different packaging. Huawei OTG tutorial (consumer.huawei.com/ph/community/details/topicId-72169/) — Huawei's own guide: plug the drive in, open the Files manager, select the photos, Copy, then Paste to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification. Huawei Backup (consumer.huawei.com/za/support/content/en-us04402235/) — Huawei's own support page: connect the phone to a USB drive via an OTG cable, go to Settings, System & updates, Backup & restore, Data backup, External storage, touch USB storage, touch BACK UP, select the data, and set a password; the data is encrypted and backed up, and the password is required to restore it — and the restore runs only through Huawei Backup on a Huawei phone; it backs up the whole device's data, not a folder of plain photo files you can open on any computer. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the five that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. MobiKin — PC drag-and-drop, a PC tool (MobiKin Assistant for Android), OTG manual copy, Files by Google, or AirDroid: the PC ways need a computer, and the phone-only ways are the same manual select-copy-paste. FoneLab — OTG manual copy in the Files app (select photos, Move or Copy to the flash drive), a PC tool (FoneLab HyperTrans, phone and drive both plugged into the computer), or Samsung Smart Switch: the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy, the PC way needs a computer, and Smart Switch is for Samsung phones, not Huawei. Cloud routes — on newer Huawei phones (Mate 30 and later) Google Photos is not preinstalled at all — those phones ship without Google services, so the cloud route is Huawei Cloud, which backs up to Huawei's servers, not to a drive you hold; on older Huawei phones with Google, Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. None of them offers an automated photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Huawei P, Mate, or nova phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Huawei phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Huawei specifics: first, there is no OTG switch to enable. Huawei's own OTG tutorial just says plug the drive in and open the Files manager — unlike OnePlus or Xiaomi there is no "OTG connection" toggle hiding in Settings. If the phone shows no reaction at all, check the USB notification: if it says the phone is charging a connected device, tap it and switch to file transfer. Second, the stock file manager on Huawei phones is Files, and the stock gallery is Gallery — and expandable storage varies by model: many recent Huawei flagships take Huawei's own NM (Nano Memory) card — the same size as a nano-SIM, in 64, 128, or 256 GB — instead of a microSD card, older models take a regular microSD card, and some have no card slot at all, so check your own model's specs. If your phone has no card slot, a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. Third, newer Huawei phones (Mate 30 and later) ship without Google services — no Google Play Store, no Google Photos preinstalled — so on those phones SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page, not from Play, and the cloud comparison is Huawei Cloud, not Google Photos. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet — and on a Huawei phone without Google Play, the APK from the GitHub release page is the way in anyway), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos — Huawei camera photos live in DCIM/Camera), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your photos live somewhere else, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 2. Plug in the USB drive. No switch to enable first — Huawei mounts the drive on its own. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 3. Tap Backup. Your whole library copies oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The copy mirrors the source folder structure on the drive, so DCIM stays DCIM. 4. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 5. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. Other apps copy originals byte-for-byte too; what SnapDisk adds is the automated whole-library run: oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, resume where it stopped, and skip-if-already-copied on the next run. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: Files (the stock route, no app needed). Huawei phones ship with the Files app as the stock file manager, and it can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive — a notification should appear; tap it to open the drive. 2. Open Files, tap the USB drive to confirm it mounted. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or tap Select all). 5. Tap Copy, then select the USB drive, and wait for the copy to finish — don't unplug the drive until Files says it's done. Use Copy, not Move: Move deletes the originals as it goes, so a bumped cable halfway through loses photos. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: you pick files one by one, there is no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time photos pile up. For a library that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

Method 3: Huawei Backup (the built-in archive). If you want Huawei's own route, the Backup app is already on the phone: connect the USB drive with an OTG cable, go to Settings, System & updates, Backup & restore, Data backup, External storage, touch USB storage, touch BACK UP, select the data you want, and follow the prompts to set a password. The data is encrypted and backed up to the drive, and the password is required to restore it — through Huawei Backup, on a Huawei phone. This works fine as a device backup. Its limits, for photos specifically: the backup is an archive, not a folder of photos — you cannot plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures; you can only restore them through Huawei Backup, and only onto a Huawei phone; and if you lose the password, the backup is unreadable. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

Method 4: through a computer (if you have one). If a PC or Mac is handy, the old route still works: plug the Huawei phone into the computer with a USB cable, tap the USB notification and choose File transfer (by default a Huawei phone charges only) — and drag the DCIM folder onto the USB drive, or use Huawei's own HiSuite on the PC to bulk-export the photos first. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Huawei Backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same archive, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: hunting for an OTG switch that isn't there (Huawei has no OTG toggle — that is a OnePlus/Xiaomi thing; if your Huawei phone ignores a drive, the switch is not the problem: check the cable or adapter, check the USB notification, and check the drive is formatted exFAT or FAT32, since stock Android cannot mount NTFS drives); mistaking an encrypted archive for a photo copy (Huawei Backup writes a backup file to the drive, not your photos as files — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not Huawei Backup; and if you do use Huawei Backup, keep the password somewhere safe, because without it the archive cannot be restored); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC, or HiSuite, needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on newer Huawei phones the cloud route is Huawei Cloud, not Google Photos — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: if you have to pick the files yourself, it isn't a backup — it's a chore you will skip. Automate the copy, check it on the drive, then delete from the phone.

### Back up LG photos to a USB drive (no computer)

LG stopped making phones in 2021, so no LG guide or LG tool will ever be written for this — and LG's own backup tools move data phone-to-phone or phone-to-PC, never phone-to-USB as plain photos. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a late LG phone. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: LG File Manager works — it is the stock file manager on LG phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; LG's own tools work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — LG Mobile Switch moves data to another phone, LG Bridge backs the phone up to a computer, and LG Backup writes a backup to an SD card or the cloud; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query is an LG-specific guide or an automated whole-library LG backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are a photo-stick product listing, generic YouTube and AnExplorer manual guides, a Dr.Fone PC tool and manual copy, or the Photos to USB app listing.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from LG to USB flash drive without computer" and every top result teaches the same generic manual job, in different packaging — none of them is written for an LG phone. Ubuy — a product listing, not a guide: a dual-connector flash drive sold as compatible with LG, Samsung, Google, and Motorola phones; it names LG among the brands and says to plug the stick in and use the phone's built-in file manager to move photos — a stick to buy, not a backup method. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the five that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. YouTube (PYcbV25CczI) — plug the drive in via OTG, open the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Move or Copy to the drive: manual select-copy-paste, and it suggests Move, which deletes the originals as it goes. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one result that is not a manual guide: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, resumes where it stopped, keeps location data, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not an LG guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. LG has no phone-side cloud of its own for this — its backup story is LG Backup to an SD card or the cloud, and LG Mobile Switch to another phone. None of them is an LG-specific guide, and none of them offers an automated LG photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an LG phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a late LG phone (G7, G8, V30 and later, Velvet, Wing, V60), or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older LG phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three LG specifics: first, there is no OTG switch to enable. Plug the drive in and the phone mounts it on its own — LG never shipped an OTG toggle. If the phone shows no reaction at all, check the USB notification: if it says the phone is charging a connected device, tap it and switch to file transfer. Second, LG left the phone business in April 2021 (wound down by July 31, 2021), so there will be no new LG phones and no new LG backup tools — and LG Mobile Switch, the phone-to-phone mover, is no longer updated and struggles on newer Android versions. The good news for storage: most LG phones have a microSD card slot, so a card is the other plug-in storage option if your phone has one — check your own model's specs. If your phone has no card in the slot, a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. Third, LG phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no Huawei-style sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos — LG camera photos live in DCIM/Camera), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your photos live somewhere else, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 2. Plug in the USB drive. No switch to enable first — LG mounts the drive on its own. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 3. Tap Backup. Your whole library copies oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The copy mirrors the source folder structure on the drive, so DCIM stays DCIM. 4. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 5. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. Other apps copy originals byte-for-byte too; what SnapDisk adds is the automated whole-library run: oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, resume where it stopped, and skip-if-already-copied on the next run. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: LG File Manager (the stock route, no app needed). LG phones ship with LG's own File Manager (open it from Management, then File Manager), and it can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Plug in the USB drive — a notification should appear; tap it to open the drive. 2. Open File Manager and tap to select the storage location — confirm the USB drive shows up. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or select all). 5. Tap Copy, then select the USB drive, and wait for the copy to finish — don't unplug the drive until File Manager says it's done. Use Copy, not Move: Move deletes the originals as it goes, so a bumped cable halfway through loses photos. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: you pick files one by one, there is no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time photos pile up. For a library that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

Method 3: LG's own tools (phone-to-phone or phone-to-PC — not phone-to-USB). If you want LG's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. LG Mobile Switch moves data from an old phone to a new LG phone over a USB cable, Wi-Fi, or an SD card — it is a migration tool, not a backup tool, and it needs a second phone on the other end. It is also no longer updated, and it struggles on newer Android versions. LG Bridge is PC software: install it on a Windows PC or Mac, plug the phone in with a USB cable, and back the phone up to the computer — a device backup to a PC, not a phone-to-USB copy. LG Backup (Settings, Backup & reset, LG Backup) backs the phone up to an SD card or the cloud — it writes a backup, not your photos as files, and you restore it through LG Backup on an LG phone. All three work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

Method 4: through a computer (if you have one). If a PC or Mac is handy, the old route still works: plug the LG phone into the computer with a USB cable, tap the USB notification and choose File transfer (by default an LG phone charges only) — and drag the DCIM folder onto the USB drive, or use LG Bridge to back the phone up to the PC first. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — LG Backup is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: hunting for an OTG switch that isn't there (LG has no OTG toggle — that is a OnePlus/Xiaomi thing; if your LG phone ignores a drive, the switch is not the problem: check the cable or adapter, check the USB notification, and check the drive is formatted exFAT or FAT32, since stock Android cannot mount NTFS drives); mistaking a backup package for a photo copy (LG Backup writes a backup to an SD card or the cloud, and LG Bridge writes a backup to the computer — not your photos as files; if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not LG Backup or LG Bridge); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC, or LG Bridge, needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on LG the cloud route is Google Photos — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: if you have to pick the files yourself, it isn't a backup — it's a chore you will skip. Automate the copy, check it on the drive, then delete from the phone.


### Back up Oppo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

Oppo's ColorOS hides one switch between you and a USB drive — OTG Connection, which turns itself off after about 10 minutes unused — and Oppo's own backup tools move photos to another phone or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On an Oppo Find X or Reno phone, turn on OTG Connection in Settings first — ColorOS switches it off again after about 10 minutes without a connected accessory — then plug a USB drive in, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: File Manager works — it is the stock file manager on Oppo phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Oppo's own tools work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — Clone Phone moves data to another phone, and HeyTap Cloud backs the phone up to the cloud; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query is an Oppo-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are one Oppo-specific manual guide, generic manual guides, PC tools, or the Photos to USB app listing.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Oppo to USB flash drive without computer" and the one Oppo-specific result is a manual guide — the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging. Coolmuster (coolmuster.com/android/transfer-files-from-oppo-to-usb-flash-drive.html) — the one Oppo-specific result: connect the drive with an OTG adapter and move files through the File Manager app, use a USB-C flash drive directly, or use the Coolmuster Android Assistant PC tool; the phone-only ways are the same manual select-copy-paste, and the third way needs a computer. FoneLab (fonelab.com) — OTG adapter plus file manager, a PC with File Explorer, or the FoneLab HyperTrans PC tool: generic Android, not written for Oppo, and two of the three ways need a computer. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the five that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. MobiKin (mobikin.com) — PC drag-and-drop, the MobiKin Assistant PC tool, OTG adapter copy, Files by Google, or AirDroid: generic Android, and three of the five ways need a computer or Wi-Fi. Oppo's own cloud is HeyTap Cloud, and it has the same limit: it backs the phone up to Oppo's servers, not to a USB drive. None of them is an Oppo-specific automated backup, and none of them offers an automated Oppo photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an Oppo phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Oppo phone (Find X, Reno, and recent A-series models), or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Oppo phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Oppo specifics: first, turn on OTG Connection before you plug anything in. ColorOS hides the switch in Settings — Additional settings on older ColorOS, System Settings on some versions, Accessibility & convenience on ColorOS 15 and newer — and if you can't find it, search Settings for "OTG". ColorOS switches the toggle off again after about 10 minutes without a connected accessory, so enable it and plug the drive in straight away; if the phone ignores the drive, the switch has probably timed out — turn it on again with the drive already attached. Not every Oppo phone has OTG at all, so if there is no OTG Connection setting anywhere, the phone may not support it. Second, Oppo's stock apps are File Manager for files and Photos for the gallery, and Oppo phones have no microSD card slot on most recent models — check your own model's specs — so a USB drive is the plug-in storage you get. Turn on OTG Connection. Open Settings, search for "OTG", and switch OTG Connection on. Do this right before plugging the drive in — ColorOS turns it off again after about 10 minutes unused. 2. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. Open File Manager and confirm the USB drive shows up as a storage location. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Method 3: Oppo's own tools (phone-to-phone or to the cloud — not phone-to-USB). If you want Oppo's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Clone Phone is Oppo's official phone-switching tool: it moves contacts, messages, photos, videos, apps, and more from an old phone to a new Oppo over Wi-Fi Direct, with no cables and no computer — but it needs a second phone on the other end, and it moves data to that phone, not to a USB drive. HeyTap Cloud is Oppo's official cloud service: turn on Cloud Backup in Settings, and it syncs contacts, photos, messages, and notes to Oppo's servers, so you can restore them on a new Oppo after a reset — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and it needs a HeyTap account and Wi-Fi. Both work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: neither of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Realme to USB flash drive without computer" and there is no Realme-specific result in the top results at all — the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the six that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=PYcbV25CczI) — a video walkthrough of the same generic route: OTG adapter, the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive; generic Android, not written for Realme. AskFilo (askfilo.com) — OTG adapter plus file manager, or a PC as a middleman; generic Android, and the second way needs a computer. Dr.Fone (drfone.wondershare.com) — four ways: Google Drive, PC drag-and-drop, OTG copy in the file manager, or AirDroid over Wi-Fi; three of the four need a computer or a cloud account, and the OTG way is the same manual file-manager copy. TheGadgetians (thegadgetians.com) — OTG adapter, the phone's file manager, select and copy to the drive; generic Android and iPhone, not written for Realme. Move Files USB/OTG/Internal (Play listing, com.fbd.moveapps.sdcard.dp) — a generic file-manager app that detects a connected OTG drive and moves files to it in bulk; a manual file manager with USB support, not an automated backup — you pick the files, and it does not promise oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, or verification. MobiKin (mobikin.com/android-backup/back-up-and-restore-realme.html) — the one Realme-specific backup guide found in the wider search, and it is not a phone-to-USB guide at all: it covers a PC tool, Google backup, HeyTap Cloud, and a local backup on the phone; no USB drive anywhere in it. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one-tap app alternative, from the wider search for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, resumes where it stopped, keeps location data, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not a Realme guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Realme's own cloud is HeyTap Cloud, and it has the same limit: it backs the phone up to Realme's servers, not to a USB drive. None of them is a Realme-specific automated backup, and none of them offers an automated Realme photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: a Realme phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Realme phone (GT, Pro, and number series), or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Realme phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Realme specifics: first, turn on OTG Connection before you plug anything in. Realme UI hides the switch in Settings — Additional settings on most versions, System Settings on some — and if you can't find it, search Settings for "OTG". Some models also offer an OTG tile in Quick Settings. Realme UI switches the toggle off again after about 10 minutes without a connected accessory, so enable it and plug the drive in straight away; if the phone ignores the drive, the switch has probably timed out — turn it on again with the drive already attached. Not every Realme phone has OTG at all, so if there is no OTG Connection setting anywhere, the phone may not support it. Second, Realme's stock file manager is File Manager, and Realme camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and whether your model has a microSD slot varies by model, so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every model. Third, Realme phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no Huawei-style sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 1: SnapDisk (one tap, background copy). SnapDisk is a free Android app that does exactly this job and nothing else. Install it from the v0.1.2 APK (it's not on Google Play yet), then: 1. Turn on OTG Connection. Open Settings, search for "OTG", and switch OTG Connection on. Do this right before plugging the drive in — Realme UI turns it off again after about 10 minutes unused. 2. Open SnapDisk and check the folders. The app opens to a settings screen with a From folder and a To folder, each with a folder picker. The defaults are already right for most people: From /sdcard/DCIM (your camera photos — Realme camera photos live in DCIM/Camera), To /disk/DCIM on the drive. If your photos live somewhere else, tap the From picker and choose that folder — the picker is the Android system folder picker, and the app keeps access to it. 3. Plug in the USB drive. SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" 4. Tap Backup. Your whole library copies oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The copy mirrors the source folder structure on the drive, so DCIM stays DCIM. 5. Watch the progress notification — real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left — with Pause and Stop. You can pause and resume any time. 6. Wait for "Backup complete." Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice — so if the free 5 GB per-run limit stops a big library partway, just run it again and it picks up where it left off. The copies are the original files. SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte from the phone to the drive — the code reads the file and writes the same bytes out, with no decode, no recompression, and no resize — and then checks that the copy on the drive is the same size as the original. Other apps copy originals byte-for-byte too; what SnapDisk adds is the automated whole-library run: oldest-first order, progress with Pause and Stop, resume where it stopped, and skip-if-already-copied on the next run. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup. The free version backs up manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. The app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

Method 2: File Manager (the stock route, no app needed). Realme phones ship with File Manager as the stock file manager, and it can copy your photos to the USB drive: 1. Turn on OTG Connection in Settings (search for "OTG" if you can't find it), then plug in the USB drive — a notification should appear; tap it to open the drive. 2. Open File Manager and confirm the USB drive shows up as a storage location — under Categories, in the Storage locations section. 3. Go back to Internal storage, DCIM, Camera, where your camera photos live. 4. Select the photos (long-press the first, tap the rest, or select all). 5. Tap Copy, then select the USB drive, and wait for the copy to finish — don't unplug the drive until File Manager says it's done. Use Copy, not Move: Move deletes the originals as it goes, so a bumped cable halfway through loses photos. This works fine for a one-off copy. Its limits are the reason SnapDisk exists: you pick files one by one, there is no progress detail beyond a spinner, no resume if you unplug mid-copy, no verification that every file actually arrived, and you have to repeat the whole manual selection next time photos pile up. For a library that grows every day, the app's oldest-first background copy is the calmer option.

Method 3: Realme's own tools (phone-to-phone, on-phone, or to the cloud — not phone-to-USB). If you want Realme's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Clone Phone is Realme's official phone-switching tool: it moves contacts, messages, photos, videos, apps, and more from an old phone to a new Realme — the new phone shows a QR code, the old phone scans it, and the data moves over a direct connection — but it needs a second phone on the other end, and it moves data to that phone, not to a USB drive. HeyTap Cloud is Realme's official cloud service: sign in with a HeyTap account, turn on Cloud Backup in Settings, and it syncs contacts, photos, messages, and notes to Realme's servers, with 5 GB free and an automatic backup about every 7 days — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and its Optimize Storage option keeps the original photos in the cloud and smaller copies on the phone, so with it on, your full-size photos may exist only in the cloud. Local Backup is Realme's on-phone backup: it stores a backup file on the phone itself, covering contacts, messages, call logs, settings, and apps — but it stays on the phone, so it is lost if the phone is reset or fails, and it is a backup file, not a folder of plain photos you can open anywhere. All three work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

Method 4: through a computer (if you have one). If a PC or Mac is handy, the old route still works: plug the Realme phone into the computer with a USB cable, tap the USB notification and choose File transfer (by default a Realme phone charges only) — and drag the DCIM folder onto the USB drive, or use a PC tool like Coolmuster Android Backup Manager or MobiKin Assistant, which both back a Realme phone up to a PC in one click. This works fine, and it is the only route above that needs a second device in between. If the phone and the drive are all you have, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — HeyTap Cloud is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: plugging the drive in before turning OTG on (on Realme, the OTG Connection switch is off by default and times out after about 10 minutes unused — that is a Realme UI thing, not a fault in the drive; if your Realme phone ignores a drive, search Settings for "OTG", turn the switch on, and plug the drive in straight away; if there is no OTG Connection setting at all, the phone may not support OTG); mistaking a phone-to-phone move for a photo copy (Clone Phone moves your photos to a new phone, HeyTap Cloud moves them to Realme's servers, and Local Backup keeps them on the same phone — none writes your photos as files to a USB drive; if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not Clone Phone, HeyTap Cloud, or Local Backup); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC, or Coolmuster Android Backup Manager, needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Realme the cloud route is Google Photos or HeyTap Cloud — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost; HeyTap Cloud's Optimize Storage has the same trap in reverse: your full-size originals may live only in the cloud); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

Rule of thumb: if you have to pick the files yourself, it isn't a backup — it's a chore you will skip. Automate the copy, check it on the drive, then delete from the phone.


### Back up Vivo photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/vivo-photos-to-usb.html

Vivo's Funtouch OS hides one switch between you and a USB drive — OTG, under Settings > More settings, which turns itself off if it is not used in 5 minutes — and Vivo's own backup tools move photos to another phone, to a PC, or to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in once the switch is on. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On a Vivo phone, turn on OTG in Settings first — Settings > More settings > OTG, and Vivo's own FAQ says the switch turns itself off if it is not used in 5 minutes — then plug a USB drive in, tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: File Manager works — it is the stock file manager on Vivo phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Vivo's own tools work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — EasyShare moves data to another phone or backs it up to a PC, and vivo Cloud backs the phone up to the cloud; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. ### Back up Honor photos to a USB drive (no computer)

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/honor-photos-to-usb.html

Honor's MagicOS has no documented OTG switch to hunt for — the drive mounts on plug-in on most models, with a "USB storage added" notification — and Honor's own backup tools write an encrypted backup package, move photos to another phone or a PC, or back them up to the cloud, never to a USB drive as plain files. A USB-C flash drive plugs straight in. Here is the manual way, and the one-tap version.

TL;DR: On an Honor phone, plug a USB drive in — most models mount it straight away with a "USB storage added" notification; if nothing appears, search Settings for "OTG" (no documented MagicOS switch location was found, and whether a switch exists or switches itself off is unverified) — then tap Backup in SnapDisk, and your whole photo library copies oldest-first to the drive in the background — with real progress (percent, GB copied / total, speed, time left), Pause and Stop, and resume where it stopped if you unplug. No computer, no upload, no account. The copies are the original files: SnapDisk streams each file byte-for-byte to the drive, never recompresses or resizes, and checks the size of every file after copying. The honest contrast, up front: Files works — it is the stock file manager on Honor phones, and it copies photos to a USB drive — but it is manual select-copy-paste with no progress detail, no resume, and no verification; Honor's own tools work too, but none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive — Backup & restore to a USB drive writes an encrypted backup package that only Honor's Backup can restore, Honor Share moves files to another Honor phone or an Honor notebook, and Honor Cloud backs the phone up to the cloud; and Google Photos backup is a cloud copy, not a USB copy. One rival app does exist — Photos to USB: OTG Backup copies a whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap and resumes where it stopped — so SnapDisk is not the only one-tap option; what it adds is oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, size verification of every file, no ads, and a free 5 GB per run with a $9.99 one-time Pro for auto-backup and unlimited size. SnapDisk copies, it never deletes — deleting from the phone afterwards is your step, only after verifying a few photos on the drive. Free version: 5 GB per run; run it again past the cap and it picks up where it stopped, because files already copied are never copied twice. As of November 16, 2026, no top search result for this query is an Honor-specific automated whole-library backup with progress, Pause/Stop, and resume: the top results are two video walkthroughs of the manual route, generic manual guides, or a rival app page.

What the search results actually offer: search "back up photos from Honor to USB flash drive without computer" and the only Honor-specific results in the top results are videos of the manual route — the rest are generic Android guides, in different packaging. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=Acqvw1-hNn8) — an Honor-specific video walkthrough of the manual route: USB OTG adapter, the phone's built-in File Manager, select photos, copy or move them to the USB drive; manual select-copy-paste, no automation. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=ySOrhwl2Kuw) — a second Honor-specific video of the same manual route: USB-C OTG adapter, File Manager, select files in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive, eject before unplugging; manual again. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=voVHMnQEfwI) — a third Honor-specific video: the same USB OTG manual copy in the Files app, or a cloud backup (Huawei Mobile Cloud, Google Drive, or OneDrive); the USB half is manual, the cloud half is not a USB copy. Pixoneye (pixoneye.com/how-to-transfer-photos-from-phone-to-usb-stick/) — copy local originals to a USB drive with a file manager, one small batch at a time; notes ThePhotoStick Omni, a dedicated stick with its own app, not an ordinary flash drive; generic Android and iPhone, not written for Honor. AnExplorer (anexplorer.io/transfer/phone-to-usb) — connect the drive with an OTG adapter, open AnExplorer, long-press to select files in DCIM/Camera, Copy, Paste to the drive: a thorough manual guide, and the only one of the six that shows a progress bar with speed and time remaining — but it is still a manual copy, with no resume or verification. YouTube (youtube.com/watch?v=PYcbV25CczI) — a video walkthrough of the same generic route: OTG adapter, the phone's built-in file manager, select photos in DCIM, Copy or Move to the drive; generic Android, not written for Honor. TheGadgetians (thegadgetians.com/how-to-transfer-files-from-phone-to-usb-without-computer/) — OTG adapter, the phone's file manager, select and copy to the drive; mentions ThePhotoStick Omni, a dedicated stick with its own app, not an ordinary flash drive; generic Android and iPhone, not written for Honor. Coolmuster (coolmuster.com/android/honor-backup-restore.html) — the one Honor-specific backup guide found in the wider search, and it is not a phone-to-USB guide at all: it covers Honor Suite (the official PC tool), Honor Cloud, and Google backup; no plain photo files on a USB drive anywhere in it. Honor's own support page (iknow-dl.service.hihonor.com) — Honor's own routes: HonorSuite to a PC, Device Clone to another phone, and Backup & restore to external storage, a USB drive or a memory card, which writes an encrypted backup package, not plain photo files; the USB route exists, but the backup it writes is a package you can only restore through Honor's Backup on an Honor phone. Honor Share (honor.com) — Honor's own support page: Honor Share moves files between Honor phones over Wi-Fi Direct, or between a phone and a computer, but only Honor notebooks with PC Manager 15.0 and above; phone-to-phone or phone-to-notebook, not phone-to-USB. Photos to USB: OTG Backup (Play listing, com.arzdrz.photos_to_usb) — the one-tap app alternative, from the wider search for this job: a real phone-to-USB app that copies the whole gallery to a pen drive in one tap, copies only new photos next time, and warns about the FAT32 4 GB limit; free with ads, with a one-time purchase to remove them. It is the closest thing to this article's job — but it is a generic Android listing, not an Honor guide, and it does not promise oldest-first order, detailed progress with Pause and Stop, or size verification of every file. Cloud routes — Google Photos backs up over Wi-Fi to Google's servers, not to a drive you hold; its "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, and a cloud backup stops working the day you stop paying for storage. Honor's own cloud is Honor Cloud, and it has the same limit: it backs the phone up to Honor's servers, not to a USB drive. None of them is an Honor-specific automated backup, and none of them offers an automated Honor photo-library backup: nothing that takes the entire camera roll, copies it oldest-first in the background as plain files you can open anywhere, shows progress, pauses and resumes, and verifies every file.

What you need: an Honor phone (Android 7.0 or later for SnapDisk); a USB drive your phone can read — a USB-C flash drive plugs straight into a modern Honor phone, or a regular USB drive with a USB-C OTG adapter; older Honor phones with a Micro-USB port need a Micro-USB OTG adapter instead; enough space on the drive for the photos you want to keep. Three Honor specifics: first, there is no OTG switch to hunt for. On most Honor phones the drive mounts on plug-in — look for a "USB storage added" or "USB drive connected" notification. If the phone ignores the drive, search Settings for "OTG": no documented MagicOS switch location was found, and whether a switch exists at all, or switches itself off, is unverified — so don't assume a missing switch means a broken phone. Not every Honor phone has OTG at all, so if there is no OTG setting anywhere, the phone may not support it. Second, Honor's stock file manager is Files, a category-based browser (Images, Videos, Documents, Audio) that integrates with Honor Cloud, and Honor camera photos live in DCIM/Camera — and whether your model has a microSD slot varies by model, so check your own model's specs rather than assuming one either way; a USB drive is the plug-in storage that works on every model. Third, Honor phones ship with Google Play, so SnapDisk installs from the v0.1.2 APK on the GitHub release page today and from Play once the listing is live — there is no Huawei-style sideload-only situation here. One format note: drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB. That only matters for very long videos — SnapDisk skips those files and lists them instead of failing the whole backup. A drive formatted exFAT has no such limit.

Method 3: Honor's own tools (encrypted backup, phone-to-phone, or to the cloud — not phone-to-USB). If you want Honor's own route, know what each tool actually does — none of them writes your photos as plain files to a USB drive. Honor's Backup & restore can write to a USB drive — Settings > System & updates > Backup & restore > Data backup > External storage > USB storage — but what it writes is an encrypted backup package, with a password you set yourself, that you can only restore through Honor's Backup on an Honor phone. It is a real USB backup, and it is the closest Honor's own tools come to this article's job — but the backup is a package, not a folder of photo files you can plug into any computer and open. Honor Share is Honor's official wireless sharing tool: it moves images, videos, and documents between Honor phones over Wi-Fi Direct, or between a phone and an Honor notebook with PC Manager 15.0 and above — but it needs a second Honor device on the other end, and it moves data to that device, not to a USB drive. Device Clone is the same idea for switching phones: it moves everything from an old phone to a new Honor phone, and again needs a second phone. Honor Cloud is Honor's official cloud service: sign in with an Honor ID and it backs the phone up to Honor's servers, automatically, with a limited free tier — but it is a cloud backup, not a USB copy, and photos sync through the Gallery app or Google Photos instead. All of them work fine for what they are. Their limit, for photos specifically: none of them gives you a folder of plain photo files on a USB drive you can plug into any computer and open. If what you want is a copy of your photos you can open anywhere, Method 1 or 2 is the route — that is the gap this article fills, as of November 16, 2026.

What this does not do: photos and videos only (SnapDisk copies image and video files; documents, voice notes, and anything that isn't a photo or video is skipped — Honor Cloud is the tool if you want contacts, messages, and settings in the same backup, not just photos); only the folder you pick (by default DCIM — your camera photos; photos in other folders only copy if you point the From folder at them, or at a parent folder that contains them); free 5 GB per run (a library bigger than 5 GB stops at the cap; run it again and it picks up where it stopped; Pro, $9.99 one-time, removes the limit and starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk); files over 4 GB on FAT32 are skipped (very long videos on a FAT32 drive are listed with their reason instead of failing the backup — reformat the drive to exFAT if you need them); it never deletes (SnapDisk only copies — freeing space on the phone is copy, check the copy on the drive, then delete the originals yourself, never the other way round).

What to avoid: hunting for an OTG switch that may not exist (no documented MagicOS switch location was found, and the Honor videos show the drive mounting on plug-in with a "USB storage added" notification; if your Honor phone ignores a drive, search Settings for "OTG" — but a missing switch is not proof the phone is broken; not every Honor phone has OTG at all); mistaking an encrypted backup for a photo copy (Honor's Backup & restore to a USB drive writes an encrypted backup package that only Honor's Backup can restore — if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not Backup & restore); mistaking a phone-to-phone move for a photo copy (Honor Share and Device Clone move your photos to a new phone or an Honor notebook, and Honor Cloud moves them to Honor's servers — none writes your photos as files to a USB drive; if you want to plug the drive into a computer and open the pictures, you need a plain copy, that is Method 1 or 2, not Honor Share, Device Clone, or Honor Cloud); PC-only tools when you have no computer (drag-and-drop through a Windows PC, or HonorSuite, needs the PC in between); cloud backup dressed as USB backup (if the app needs an account and an upload before your photos are safe, that's a cloud subscription with a USB step; on Honor the cloud route is Google Photos or Honor Cloud — and Google Photos' "Storage saver" setting compresses photos, which is the one place quality actually gets lost); deleting before verifying (copy, open a few photos on the drive, then delete from the phone — never the other way round; SnapDisk only copies, it never deletes, so the delete step is always yours, and always after the check); moving instead of copying (the file manager's Move option copies and then deletes the originals in one step — if the copy fails halfway, photos are already gone from the phone; copy first, verify, then delete); unplugging mid-copy (pulling a USB drive out while files are still writing can corrupt the file in flight — wait for the copy to finish, or pause it first).

### SnapDisk FAQ

https://dzianisv.github.io/photo-backup/faq.html

The questions a first visitor asks about backing up photos to a USB disk with SnapDisk — answered from how the app actually works in v0.1.2.

TL;DR: SnapDisk backs up your photos to a USB disk — plug it in, tap Backup in the notification, and your photos copy oldest-first in the background, with live progress and Pause / Stop. The free version covers 5 GB per run; Pro is a one-time $9.99 for auto-backup on connect and unlimited size. Nothing is uploaded anywhere: the app has no internet permission, so your photos physically cannot leave your device.

How does SnapDisk back up my photos? Plug in a USB disk and SnapDisk offers a backup in a notification: "External storage is connected. Backup photos?" Tap Backup and your photos and videos copy oldest-first — your earliest photos first — in the background, while you use the phone normally. The progress notification shows real percent, copied / total size, speed, and time left, with Pause and Stop. Every file is size-verified after copying, so the counts are proof, not a promise. Files that already copied are never copied twice.

How much can I back up for free? The free version backs up photos and videos manually, up to 5 GB per backup run, with no ads, no account, and no cloud. SnapDisk Pro is a one-time $9.99 purchase (no subscription) that starts the backup automatically when you plug in a disk and removes the size limit. There is no subscription and no monthly fee — Pro is paid once.

Does SnapDisk upload my photos anywhere? No. Copying runs entirely on your device, from your internal storage to the external disk you choose. The app has no internet permission, so your photos cannot leave your device. It works with the phone in airplane mode — if a backup works in airplane mode, it is offline, and SnapDisk does.

What happens if I unplug the disk mid-copy? The backup pauses with the full error shown and resumes where it stopped when the disk is back. A partially copied file resumes from where it stopped instead of starting over, and files that already copied are never copied twice. If a file is corrupt or too big for FAT32, it's retried once, then skipped with its reason listed — it never stalls the whole backup.

What disk formats work? Drives formatted exFAT have no per-file size limit. Drives formatted FAT32 can't hold a single file over 4 GB — that only matters for very long videos. SnapDisk skips those files, lists them with the reason, and keeps going instead of failing the whole backup. NTFS has not been tested on a real disk yet, so we make no claim about it either way: not supported, not unsupported — untested.

Where do my photos go on the disk? By default SnapDisk copies from /sdcard/DCIM on your phone to /disk/DCIM on the external disk. Both folders can be changed in Settings — open the app and pick your own From and To folders. The app opened is a settings screen only; the backup itself is started from the notification.

Is SnapDisk on Google Play yet? Not yet — the Play listing is being prepared. Until then, install the v0.1.2 APK from the GitHub release page. It needs Android 7.0 or later.

Something does not work. Where do I report it? Open an issue on GitHub — every report gets an answer: github.com/dzianisv/photo-backup/issues. If a backup fails, the app shows the full error — copy it into the issue so the cause is visible, not guessed.
